title: Consumption modeling & fallback strategy - Northstar Logistics
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment
summary: Discovery focused on consumption economics for a high-throughput logistics inference use case. Customer runs multi-turn routing/ETA model and needs predictable unit costs; discussed per-token and per-call levers (batching, KV/prefix cache, quantization) and tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated reserved capacity and Private VPC. Action items: pricing workbook, pilot scope + benchmark plan, security & SOC2 docs.
action_items: Jordan Patel - Share per-token economic workbook + sample calculus for 3 model sizes - due 2026-12-08
Priya Menon - Draft pilot benchmark plan (throughput + 95th p99 latency targets) - due 2026-12-10
Michael Chen - Provide representative traffic profile (seq length distribution + concurrency) - due 2026-12-09
next_steps: Redwood to send pricing workbook and cached-batching recommendations
Schedule 2-hour pilot kickoff next week for benchmarking on a dedicated pool
Customer to circulate budget/approval timeline to procurement and infra
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05 16:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (Northstar Head of ML), Sara Lopez (CTO), Luis Ortega (Infra)

Summary: Short discovery to map Northstar's consumption profile and see which hosting mode and levers make sense given their budget ceiling and latency SLOs.

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick round robin?
00:10 Michael: Hey Jordan, Michael here. we run a mix of chatty routing, um, and short prompt classification for driver ETA and re-routing. typical request is like 3 to 8 turns, sometimes longer if the customer asks follow-ups.
00:25 Sara: Sara here. i'm mostly curious about cost predictability and what it looks like if we go hosted vs, uh, dedicated GPU pool behind a commit. Security is another big one.
00:38 Jordan: Great. Priya from engineering will walk through the batching/caching levers after i sketch the econ model. Priya?
00:45 Priya: hi all. quick note, i might refer to the KV cache as "K-V cash" in the transcription, excuse any typos. so we typically look at three levers: batching (how many requests we combine), prefix or KV cache (replay tokens already cached), and model quantization/variant selection.
01:05 Luis: for infra: our traffic is spiky midday, concurrency peaks at ~120 req/s, avg token length per request is ~180 tokens, but some heavy detailed queries go to 1k tokens.
01:20 Jordan: ok that's super helpful. so at a rough level per-token hosted pricing + dynamic batching can get you to X cents per token, while dedicated reserved capacity reduces effective per-token when utilization is high but requires a commit. have you got a budget cap for monthly inference spend?
01:40 Michael: we have a soft cap of $40k/mo for the first 6 months of rollout. we can expand if results are positive.
01:48 Jordan: good anchor. for that $40k, we need to map throughput and model size. two common patterns: if you prefer predictable latency SLOs (p95 under 250ms) dedicated with reserved capacity or private deployment is easier; if you can tolerate a little variance, hosted with auto-burst is cheapest to start.
02:10 Priya: and on batching: continuous batching offers better GPU utilization but adds a small latency tail. we can do small windows (20-40ms) to preserve latency. for your median 180-token requests, batching 8-12 can drop per-token GPU cost by 30-45% depending on model.
02:34 Sara: what about prefix caching, is that only for repeated prompts? we have a lot of similar route planning queries so maybe it helps.
02:42 Priya: yes, prefix cache stores KV state for repeated context; for multi-turn dialogs with similar prefixes you can see big wins. in practice we observed 25-60% token savings for routing-like patterns. note caches work best on dedicated pools or private because eviction / cross-tenant reuse is different in hosted.
03:10 Michael: that eviction bit, do you offer deterministic cache residency? we have privacy constraints.
03:18 Jordan: in Dedicated/Private, we provide customer-isolated caches and strict TTLs, plus ability to pin keys for sessions. Hosted can't guarantee cross-tenant pinning but still yields savings via our per-customer cache namespace.
03:34 Luis: on the dedicated pricing, do we pay per GPU hour or per-token on top? how's the math?
03:40 Jordan: Dedicated is subscription for reserved GPUs (monthly commit). the economics model we send shows amortized per-token if you run at X% utilization. e.g., a mid-size 8-GPU pool at 70% utilization could map to about 0.0009-0.0012 USD per token for a 7B model workload after batching/caching. hosted per-token may be 20-40% higher but no upfront commit.
04:10 Michael: rough calc — with $40k/mo, what throughput can we support?
04:15 Jordan: depends on your batching and caching. if we assume 180 tokens per request, 120 req/s peak, and 30% cache hit, you can model effective token/sec and multiply by per-token. we'll send a workbook that makes this explicit; the short answer is that with 30% cache and moderate batching you can likely operate a 7B model at that budget but you'd need dedicated pool to guarantee p95 latency.
05:00 Priya: also quantization: 4-bit/INT4 runner reduces GPU memory and cost and can enable higher batch sizes. quality tradeoff varies by model, we'd recommend an eval on your prompt set.
05:20 Sara: is quantization something you manage or we do locally?
05:24 Priya: Redwood's runtime supports quantized kernels and we can run the model in quantized mode in both Hosted and Dedicated; for Private we ship the runtime and ops can run it with your infra and KMS.
05:40 Michael: talk me through fallback policies. we want worst-case guarantees rather than outages.
05:46 Jordan: common approach: primary route to high-quality model; fallback to smaller model variant or cached response when latency or capacity thresholds breach. Redwood supports rule-based routing (latency-first, cost-first) and automatic fallback to compatible model variants in the same family. we can set thresholds so that if p95 > 350ms for 30s triggers fallback.
06:15 Luis: so we could have a heavy 13B for complex planning and a 3-7B for routine routing?
06:21 Priya: exactly. and with prefix caches, often the smaller model is enough for most tokens; you can also do hybrid where the heavy model runs only on cold-starts or long-horizon planning.
06:38 Michael: security questions: we need SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS with customer-managed keys, and audit logs. can you support that in Hosted?
06:50 Jordan: Hosted: SOC2 is available (we'll send the attestation), SSO/SAML via SAML2, and customer-managed KMS is offered for Dedicated and Private; Hosted can integrate with a bring-your-key pattern in select regions but for strict KMS/HSM you’ll want Private. audit logs and token-level tracing are available across tiers; Private gives you direct log access.
07:20 Sara: VPC peering for Private — is that a thing or do we need on-prem install?
07:25 Priya: we support VPC peering and private control plane; for fully air-gapped you can take the on-prem package. VPC peering gives direct network path and you keep your keys.
07:40 Michael: procurement will ask for an SLA. do you offer SLOs for Dedicated?
07:45 Jordan: yes Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; we can include that in the contract. Hosted has best-effort SLAs but we can offer higher support tiers.
07:58 Luis: back to budget — if we wanted headroom for bursts above 120 req/s, how does burst capacity pricing work?
08:06 Jordan: we offer burst capacity on Dedicated as a paid add-on; you can reserve baseline and enable burst credits billed by GPU-hour or token slice. Burst pricing tends to be lower than on-demand hosted for the same hardware because it's negotiated.
08:25 Michael: what's a realistic pilot scope? we want to test both econ and quality.
08:30 Priya: recommended pilot: 2 weeks on a small dedicated pool (2-4 GPUs), mirror production traffic at ~20% scale, run synthetic spike tests, measure p50/p95/p99 and token burn, evaluate cache hit rates, and test fallback routing.
08:50 Jordan: we'll size the pilot so cost fits within a small pilot budget; we can also do a hosted-run A/B if you prefer zero commit.
09:00 Sara: procurement will probably push for hosted initially due to procurement speed. Any suggestions for internal sell?
09:05 Jordan: show them the amortized per-token vs projected usage in the workbook and highlight risk reduction with dedicated (predictability + SLA). we can also provide a 30-day pilot discount to reduce friction.
09:20 Michael: any gotchas on billing or hidden token counts? e.g., system prompts or hidden prefix tokens?
09:26 Priya: good callout. we bill on the model tokens returned and consumed, and system/prefix tokens are included. we expose detailed usage with token breakdown so you can map where spend is going. caching will reduce billed tokens if prefix reused.
09:45 Luis: curious about multi-tenant cache behavior in Hosted — do you ever evict based on other users?
09:50 Priya: in Hosted we isolate namespaces but eviction policies depend on global memory pressure; we try to give per-customer guarantees but cannot pin indefinitely like Dedicated. that's why customers with strict residency / cache pinning choose Dedicated/Private.
10:10 Jordan: okay let's move to wrap with explicit next steps.
10:15 Michael: quick interjection — competitor question: we have POC quotes from BigCloud AI and OnPremCo who propose an on-prem install with big upfront cost; how do you compare?
10:26 Jordan: OnPremCo is heavy on upfront capex; Redwood Dedicated is middle ground with predictable monthly commits and less ops; BigCloud AI tends to be similar to hosted providers but our specialized runtime and batching gives you better per-token economics for certain workloads. we'll put a comparison in the workbook.
10:45 Sara: can you share examples of caching hit patterns for logistics customers? numbers would help.
10:50 Priya: yes — in previous routing customers we saw 35-55% token savings from prefix caching, and batching improved throughput by 30-50% depending on request size. we'll share anonymized examples.
11:10 Jordan: recap: Jordan to send econ workbook + competitor comparison, Priya to draft pilot benchmark and caching recommendations, Michael to send traffic profile. redwood will propose pilot sizing and a 2-week runbook.
11:28 Michael: sounds good, we'll look for the workbook.
11:33 Sara: thanks all.
11:35 Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invite for pilot kickoff.

End of transcript.
